summary: Defines how to use Internationalized Resource Identifiers and URIs to identify or interact with entities on the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This sets how to write a clickable link that points to a chat address or action on an XMPP chat service.

questions: difference between xmpp: and xmpp:// links
how to percent encode an xmpp address
subtitle: How to write a chat address or an action on an XMPP service as an xmpp: link that other software can understand.

tldr.problem: Software outside an XMPP network, such as web browsers, calendars and databases, needs a standard way to point at XMPP entities, but native XMPP addresses must not carry a URI scheme.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the xmpp scheme for IRIs and URIs: an optional authority to log in as, a path holding the XMPP address, and an optional query that suggests an action such as ?message. It also spells out how to convert between a native address, an IRI and a URI.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4622 and fixes its errors by requiring more characters to be percent-encoded, and it registers the xmpp URI scheme as permanent.

today: RFC 5122 is a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 4622. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why XMPP Needs Links
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is a streaming XML technology. Two entities on a network use it to exchange XML elements called stanzas at a rate close to real time.

Inside an XMPP network, an address must not be prepended with a URI scheme. Applications outside the network still need to name XMPP entities. The RFC gives examples: databases that store XMPP addresses, and non-native user agents such as web browsers and calendaring applications.

An XMPP address is very close to being an IRI without a scheme. There is no freestanding registry of IRI schemes, so the RFC defines XMPP identifiers mainly as URIs and registers an xmpp URI scheme. It specifies how to identify and interact with XMPP entities, defines the syntax, and defines how to turn IRIs into URIs and back.
sections.plainLanguage: Chat programs have their own address book, but other programs, like a web browser, need a way to write those addresses down. This RFC invents a standard way to write them as links.

sections.title: Why a New Scheme
sections.content:
XMPP instant messaging and presence applications must already handle im: and pres: URIs. But XMPP is also used for network management, workflow systems, generic publish-subscribe, remote procedure calls, content syndication, gaming and middleware, and those do not implement instant messaging semantics. A generic XMPP entity also does not implement the semantics of http:, ftp: or mailto:. So a new scheme is needed to identify or interact with any XMPP entity.

The scheme is for non-native interfaces and applications. Inside XMPP, for example in the to or from attribute of a stanza, an entity MUST still be addressed as [node@]domain[/resource] with no scheme.

The scheme is defined mainly for identification rather than interaction. When an application does resolve a link that carries suggested interaction, it is expected to generate an XMPP stanza and send it to the identified resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Other link types like web links or email links do not fit a chat address. So a brand new kind of link was made just for XMPP.

sections.title: The Form of an XMPP IRI
sections.content:
A native XMPP address is a string of Unicode characters, encoded as UTF-8, of the form [ node "@" ] domain [ "/" resource ]. The node and resource parts use distinct stringprep profiles, and the domain follows internationalized domain name rules.

An XMPP IRI is the xmpp scheme and a colon, then either an authority-and-path or just a path, then an optional ? query and an optional fragment after a number sign. The path is an optional node followed by @, a host, and an optional / resource. The simplest example in the RFC is xmpp:node@example.com.

Some characters are legal in XMPP but not in the matching part of an IRI or URI. In node identifiers these are [ \ ] ^ ` { | }. In resource identifiers they are " < > [ \ ] ^ ` { | }. They MUST be percent-encoded when an XMPP address becomes an XMPP IRI or URI.

The URI syntax is given separately in the IANA registration, because IANA recognizes only URI schemes. Converting an IRI to a URI MUST follow Section 3.1 of RFC 3987.
sections.plainLanguage: The link starts with the word xmpp and a colon, then the chat address. A few tricky characters have to be written in a special code so they do not confuse the link.

sections.title: Authority, Path, Query and Fragment
sections.content:
The authority component starts with //. Its presence tells the processing application to authenticate as the node@domain given there, rather than as a configured account. Without it, the application authenticates as a configured user at a configured XMPP server. If the application has default credentials, it SHOULD ignore the authority component.

The difference is easy to miss. xmpp://guest@example.com means authenticate as guest@example.com. xmpp:guest@example.com only identifies the node. A link such as xmpp://guest@example.com/support@example.com?message authenticates as guest and sends a message to support@example.com.

The path holds the XMPP address to which a stanza is eventually directed. It can name a node and resource, as in xmpp:example-node@example.com/some-resource, or only a server, as in xmpp:example.com.

The query carries a query type plus optional key-value pairs, for example xmpp:example-node@example.com?message;subject=Hello%20World. Pairs are separated by ; rather than &, to avoid escaping problems in HTML and XML. An application that does not understand the query type MUST ignore the whole query, and one that does not know a key MUST ignore that key and its value. Query types and keys are tracked in a registry run by the XMPP Registrar function of the XMPP Standards Foundation, and applications SHOULD submit theirs there.

The fragment has unknown, unconstrained semantics, because an XMPP resource offers no media type. An application that does not understand it MUST ignore it.

The RFC says the authority form is unlikely to be used in most links. User agents SHOULD discourage people from typing the //.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the link as an envelope. The address says who it is for, the query says what you want to do, like send a message, and the part after two slashes says who you log in as.

sections.title: Generating a Link from an Address
sections.content:
To build an XMPP IRI, the generating application MUST first make sure the address follows the XMPP core rules, including UTF-8 and the stringprep profiles. Because an IRI contains the original Unicode characters, it then MUST decode the UTF-8 back to Unicode. Then it concatenates, in order: xmpp:; optionally //, an authority and /; optionally the node and @; the host; optionally / and the resource; optionally ? and a query; optionally a number sign and a fragment.

Several characters allowed in a native address are delimiters in an IRI, so they MUST be percent-encoded. These are the number sign and ? in nodes, and /, ?, the number sign, @ and the space character in resources. The RFC walks through a deliberately nasty node and resource to show the result.

The worked example starts from the Czech address jiri@cechy.example/v Praze, written with accented letters. The IRI keeps the accented characters and encodes the space as %20. The URI form encodes the non-ASCII characters too, giving xmpp:ji%C5%99i@%C4%8Dechy.example/v%20Praze.
sections.plainLanguage: To make the link, you write the address down and swap awkward characters, like a space, for a short code such as %20, so the link stays in one piece.

sections.title: Processing a Link
sections.content:
A processing application given a URI MUST first convert it to an IRI using Section 3.2 of RFC 3987. It then separates the scheme, the authority if any, the address, the query if any and the fragment if any. It MUST check that the resulting address follows the XMPP core rules.

The application then either handles the rest itself or invokes a helper. The likely steps are:

  • Connect to an XMPP server if not already connected, as the authority user or as the configured user.
  • Optionally find out what kind of entity the recipient is.
  • Optionally show a suitable interface based on the recipient or the query.
  • Build a stanza from the user or application input.
  • Send it over the authenticated connection to the recipient.

The RFC notes that the first two steps resemble HTTP authentication, and the last three resemble handling a mailto: link. Percent-encoded octets for the special characters MUST be turned back into the characters they stand for, so %20 becomes a space in the final address.
sections.plainLanguage: When your computer sees the link, it logs in to the chat service, shows you a box to type in, and then sends your message to the right address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the IRI, URI and XMPP core documents all apply. The RFC adds six specific points.

  • Reliability. Accounts can be removed, so a link to a node may not always point at the same owner. Resource links are even more ephemeral, since a resource is usually tied to a temporary session. Server and service links are typically the most reliable.
  • Malicious construction. Port numbers are prohibited in these links, since ports are found through DNS SRV records, which makes malicious links less likely.
  • Back-end transcoding. Harmful dereferencing is unlikely. XMPP servers SHOULD NOT natively parse these links but accept only the XML wire protocol.
  • Sensitive information. Publishing links on websites may help attackers harvest addresses. Passwords and other credentials are forbidden in the authority component, and SASL ANONYMOUS can be used if desired.
  • Semantic attacks. People may expect // after every scheme, so applications MUST clearly tell xmpp://guest@example.com from xmpp:guest@example.com.
  • Spoofing. Allowing the full range of Unicode makes look-alike addresses easier, as with other IRIs, so applications showing links to people must follow best practices against address mimicking.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can trick people, for example by looking like a friend's address when it is not. So programs must be careful, never put passwords in the link, and make clear what a link will do.

sections.title: Registering the xmpp URI Scheme
sections.content:
Section 3 is the IANA registration template for the xmpp scheme. Its status is permanent. The scheme identifies entities that natively communicate using XMPP and is mainly used for identification rather than location. An application that enables interaction MUST follow Section 2 to rebuild the address, connect to a suitable server and send a suitable stanza. There is no MIME type for the scheme.

The scheme is meant for interfaces to an XMPP network from non-native user agents such as web browsers, and for applications that need to identify XMPP entities as full URIs or IRIs. The RFC reports no known interoperability concerns, and the scheme is registered in the IETF tree, so the IETF keeps change control.

Section 4 says this document obsoletes the registration created by RFC 4622. Appendix A lists what changed: the extra characters in node and resource identifiers that must be percent-encoded, the corrected ABNF and the updated examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC puts the new link type on the official list, so everyone agrees xmpp: links are a real, permanent kind of link.

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF AN XMPP LINK

items.title: Authority
items.text: After //. Names the account to log in as, for example xmpp://guest@example.com.

items.title: Path
items.text: The XMPP address itself, such as xmpp:node@example.com/some-resource.

items.title: Query
items.text: A query type with optional ;key=value pairs, such as ?message;subject=Hello%20World.

items.title: Fragment
items.text: Semantics left to each application, which MUST ignore it if not understood.
